Moses encourages Israel and Joshua (verses 1–8)

Moses assured Israel that God would continue to be present with the people.

The apostle applies this promise to God's spiritual Israel, giving every believer strong reason for faith and hope.

The gospel is preached to us as well: the Lord will never fail or abandon his people (Hebrews 13:5).

Moses presented Joshua as Israel's next leader.

The people already knew his wisdom, courage and affection.

God himself had appointed Joshua and would acknowledge and bless his leadership.

Joshua gladly received Moses' instruction to be strong and courageous.

Anyone who has God on their side should be bold.

Through him we can act bravely and overcome.

When we resist the devil, he will flee from us.

Reading the law aloud every seventh year (verses 9–13)

We should read God's word privately, but we must not think it unnecessary to hear it read publicly.

The law was to be read solemnly during the year of release.

That year pictured the grace of the gospel, the acceptable year of the Lord.

Forgiveness and freedom through Christ give us powerful reasons to obey his commands.

The law was to be read to all Israel: men, women, children and foreigners.

Everyone should become familiar with God's word, because its commands apply to everyone.

Those who remember how hard people once worked to obtain even fragments of Scripture should feel grateful that whole copies are so widely available today.

For many centuries, Israelites had lived under very different conditions.

Yet human hearts are naturally so careless that even abundant access to Scripture may not be enough to preserve the knowledge of God's truths, commands and worship.

Israel's future rebellion is foretold (verses 14–22)

Moses and Joshua stood before the divine Majesty at the entrance of the tabernacle.

The Lord reminded Moses that he would soon die.

Even people who are prepared and willing to die may benefit from being reminded of its approach.

God also foretold that Israel would break the covenant Moses had worked so hard to establish.

The people would abandon the Lord.

Then, in righteous judgment, he would abandon them.

Moses was instructed to give the people a song that would remain as a permanent witness.

It would testify for God, showing he had faithfully warned them, and against Israel, showing the people had neglected the warning.

God's word exposes the thoughts and intentions of the human heart.

Ministers who preach it cannot know all their listeners' thoughts.

But the God whose word they proclaim understands those thoughts perfectly.

The book of the law is entrusted to the Levites (verses 23–30)

Moses solemnly handed over the book of the law to the Levites.

It was to be placed in—or, more precisely, beside—the ark.

The song recorded in the next chapter was given to Moses and then to Israel.

He first wrote it as the Holy Spirit instructed him, then spoke it aloud before the people.

Moses warned that he knew they would become corrupt after his death.

That prospect must have caused him deep sorrow.

Yet he could take comfort in knowing that he had performed his duty.

God's glory would not fail, whether revealed through Israel's settlement in the promised land or through its dispersion.

The foundation of God's work remains secure.
classic_reading:
[Deut.31.1-Deut.31.8]
Chapter 31
Chapter Outline
Moses encourages the people, and Joshua. | (1-8) |
The law to be read every seventh year. | (9-13) |
The Israelites' apostacy foretold, A song given to be witness against them. | (14-22) |
The law delivered to the Levites. | (22-30) |
Verses 1-8
Moses assures Israel of the constant presence of God with them. This is applied by the apostle to all God's spiritual Israel, to encourage their faith and hope; unto us is this gospel preached, as well as unto them; he will never fail thee, nor forsake thee, [Heb.13.5] He 13:5. Moses commends Joshua to them for a leader; one whose wisdom, and courage, and affection they had long known; one whom God had appointed to be their leader; and therefore would own and bless. Joshua is well pleased to be admonished by Moses to be strong and of good courage. Those shall speed well, who have God with them; therefore they ought to be of good courage. Through God let us do valiantly, for through him we shall do victoriously; if we resist the devil, he will flee from us.
[Deut.31.9-Deut.31.13]
Verses 9-13
Though we read the word in private, we must not think it needless to hear it read in public. This solemn reading of the law must be done in the year of release. The year of release was typical of gospel grace, which is called the acceptable year of the Lord; for our pardon and liberty by Christ, engage us to keep his commandments. It must be read to all Israel, men, women, children, and to the strangers. It is the will of God that all people should acquaint themselves with his word. It is a rule to all, therefore should be read to all. Whoever has read of the pains taken by many persons to get scraps of the Scriptures, when a whole copy could not be obtained, or safely possessed, will see how thankful we should be for the thousands of copies amongst us. They will also understand the very different situation in which the Israelites were placed for many ages. But the heart of man is so careless, that all will be found too little, to keep up a knowledge of the truths, precepts, and worship of God.
[Deut.31.14-Deut.31.22]
Verses 14-22
Moses and Joshua attended the Divine Majesty at the door of the tabernacle. Moses is told again that he must shortly die; even those who are most ready and willing to die, need to be often reminded of its coming. The Lord tells Moses, that, after his death, the covenant he had taken so much pains to make between Israel and their God, would certainly be broken. Israel would forsake Him; then God would forsake Israel. Justly does he cast those off who so unjustly cast him off. Moses is directed to deliver them a song, which should remain a standing testimony for God, as faithful to them in giving them warning, and against them, as persons false to themselves in not taking the warning. The word of God is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of men's hearts, and meets them by reproofs and correction. Ministers who preach the word, know not the imaginations of men; but God, whose word it is, knows perfectly.
[Deut.31.23-Deut.31.30]
Verses 23-30
The solemn delivery of the book of the law to the Levites, to be deposited in, or rather by the side, of the ark, is again related. The song which follows in the next chapter is delivered to Moses, and by him to the people. He wrote it first, as the Holy Spirit taught him; and then spake it in the hearing of all the people. Moses tells them plainly, I know that after my death ye will utterly corrupt yourselves. Many a sad thought, no doubt, it occasioned to this good man; but his comfort was, that he had done his duty, and that God would be glorified in their dispersion, if not in their settlement, for the foundation of God stands sure.

Original chapter outline — explicit verse-label correctionsOriginal outlineVersesThe song of Moses.1, 2The character of God, The character of Israel.3–6The great things God had done for Israel.7–14The wickedness of Israel.15–18The judgments which would come upon them for their sins.19–25Deserved vengeance withheld.26–38God's deliverance for his people.39–43The exhortation with which the song was delivered.44–47Moses to go up mount Nebo to die.48–52
Moses' song begins (verses 1 and 2)

Moses called heaven and earth to witness the truth and importance of what he was about to declare.

His teaching was the gospel: God's message about Jesus Christ, grace and mercy through him, and salvation and life received through him.

God's perfection and Israel's character (verses 3–6)

God is called a Rock here.

Henry notes that this is the first time Scripture uses that name for him.

The image expresses God's unchangeable power, faithfulness and love, revealed in Christ and the gospel.

We may build our hope upon that sure foundation and find shelter in him against enemies, burning heat and storms.

God's work is perfect.

This includes the saving work in which every divine perfection is displayed.

His dealings with creatures are directed by wisdom that cannot make mistakes and by flawless justice.

No one will suffer injustice at his hand.

The song also brings a serious charge against Israel.

Even God's children have faults and sinful stains while they remain in this imperfect life.

Anyone claiming complete freedom from sin is deceiving himself.

But Henry distinguishes the failings of God's children from a settled, notorious and unrepentant practice of sin, which he regards as a mark of the devil's children.

Israel acted foolishly in abandoning divine mercy for worthless idols.

God's extraordinary care for Israel (verses 7–14)

Moses recalled particular examples of the Lord's goodness toward Israel.

The eagle caring for her young was a beautiful picture of Christ's love.

Christ placed himself between God's justice and our guilty souls, bearing our sins in his body upon the tree.

Through gospel preaching and the Holy Spirit's power, he awakens sinners and draws them away from Satan's bondage.

The imagery in verses 13 and 14 also pictures believers overcoming their spiritual enemies—sin, Satan and the world—through Christ.

In him they are safe and victorious.

When their hearts are set above earthly affairs, they enjoy spiritual peace and joy.

Henry looks forward to such blessings for spiritual Israel in the latter days.

Israel abandons its Savior (verses 15–18)

Moses described two forms of Israel's wickedness, both involving apostasy.

The people were called Jeshurun.

Henry notes alternative explanations of the name: some interpret it as upright people, others as seeing people.

Israel soon lost the reputation for both righteousness and knowledge.

The people indulged bodily appetite as though their only task was to satisfy the flesh.

Proud and self-indulgent people effectively make gods of themselves and their appetites.

They turn away from the Lord and treat him as unimportant.

Henry insists that sinners have only one way of being accepted and sanctified before God.

False religion may commend other routes and call this openness, but that does not make those routes valid.

How foolish it is to forsake the Rock of salvation for the rock of ruin!

God's judgments against sin (verses 19–25)

The previous lines described Israel's rebellion.

These lines describe the judgments God's justice would bring.

We deceive ourselves if we think people may reject him while he remains indifferent.

Sin is hateful before the holy God.

We should see the harm it causes and reject the folly of laughing at it.

God withholds the vengeance Israel deserved (verses 26–38)

Israel's idolatry and rebellion deserved destruction.

Yet the Lord spared the nation.

Henry regards the preservation of the Jewish people as a continuing witness to Scripture's truth and as part of God's wise and holy purposes.

The prophecies, he says, give some idea of those purposes.

God will not allow his glorious throne to be dishonored.

It is wise to consider the end of one's life.

Such consideration often helps sinners return to him.

The passage speaks particularly about God's purpose for Israel in the latter days, but the warning applies more widely.

What happiness will sinners lose, and what misery will they encounter, if they continue rebelling against God?

“What will be the end of it?” (Jeremiah 5:31).

God will bring down his church's enemies at the time he chooses.

People who imagine themselves completely secure may suddenly be destroyed.

And the moment of greatest distress for God's people may be the moment when he appears to rescue them.

Anyone trusting in a refuge other than God will find that false refuge fail when it is needed most.

Henry understands the Jewish rejection of the Messiah as a continuation of Israel's earlier idolatry, apostasy and rebellion.

He anticipates a future humbling and repentance, followed by faith in the Mediator they have rejected and renewed deliverance and prosperity.

These are Henry's theological interpretations of the historical nation and prophecy, preserved as his words rather than asserted as new editorial judgments.

The Lord delivers his people (verses 39–43)

The end of the song contains three messages.

First, glory belongs to God. No one can escape his power.

Second, it brings terror to his enemies. God's judgment comes against those who hate him.

Third, it brings comfort to his own people. The song ends with joy.

Whatever judgments fall on sinners, those who belong to God will be cared for.

Moses urges Israel to remember the song (verses 44–47)

Moses delivered the song solemnly.

He charged Israel to remember all the good words God had spoken through him.

These matters are not trivial.

They concern life and death.

To heed them is to find everlasting life; to disregard them is to face ruin.

How good it would be if everyone were convinced that faith is the very life of the soul!

Moses is commanded to die on Nebo (verses 48–52)

Moses had completed his work.

Why should he desire to stay longer in this world?

God reminded him of the sin that had prevented him from entering Canaan.

Even the best believers should approach death with repentance for the sins and weaknesses they still remember.

But they may die peacefully whenever God calls them.

A sure hope of eternal life beyond death, founded on faith, allows them to do so even though they remember their faults.
classic_reading:
[Deut.32.1-Deut.32.2]
Chapter 32
Chapter Outline
The song of Moses. | (1-2) |
The character of God, The character of Israel. | (3-6) |
The great things God had done for Israel. | (7-14) |
The wickedness of Israel. | (19-25) |
The judgments which would come upon them for their sins. | (15-18) |
Deserved vengeance withheld. | (26-38) |
God's deliverance for his people. | (39-43) |
The exhortation with which the song was delivered. | (44-47) |
Moses to go up mount Nebo to die. | (48-52) |
Verses 1-2
Moses begins with a solemn appeal to heaven and earth, concerning the truth and importance of what he was about to say. His doctrine is the gospel, the speech of God, the doctrine of Christ; the doctrine of grace and mercy through him, and of life and salvation by him.
[Deut.32.3-Deut.32.6]
Verses 3-6
"He is a Rock." This is the first time God is called so in Scripture. The expression denotes that the Divine power, faithfulness, and love, as revealed in Christ and the gospel, form a foundation which cannot be changed or moved, on which we may build our hopes of happiness. And under his protection we may find refuge from all our enemies, and in all our troubles; as the rocks in those countries sheltered from the burning rays of the sun, and from tempests, or were fortresses from the enemy. "His work is perfect:" that of redemption and salvation, in which there is a display of all the Divine perfection, complete in all its parts. All God's dealings with his creatures are regulated by wisdom which cannot err, and perfect justice. He is indeed just and right; he takes care that none shall lose by him. A high charge is exhibited against Israel. Even God's children have their spots, while in this imperfect state; for if we say we have no sin, no spot, we deceive ourselves. But the sin of Israel was not habitual, notorious, unrepented sin; which is a certain mark of the children of Satan. They were fools to forsake their mercies for lying vanities. All wilful sinners, especially sinners in Israel, are unwise and ungrateful.
[Deut.32.7-Deut.32.14]
Verses 7-14
Moses gives particular instances of God's kindness and concern for them. The eagle's care for her young is a beautiful emblem of Christ's love, who came between Divine justice and our guilty souls, and bare our sins in his own body on the tree. And by the preached gospel, and the influences of the Holy Spirit, He stirs up and prevails upon sinners to leave Satan's bondage. In ver. #(13-14), are emblems of the conquest believers have over their spiritual enemies, sin, Satan, and the world, in and through Christ. Also of their safety and triumph in him; of their happy frames of soul, when they are above the world, and the things of it. This will be the blessed case of spiritual Israel in every sense in the latter day.
[Deut.32.15-Deut.32.18]
Verses 15-18
Here are two instances of the wickedness of Israel, each was apostacy from God. These people were called Jeshurun, "an upright people," so some; "a seeing people," so others: but they soon lost the reputation both of their knowledge and of their righteousness. They indulged their appetites, as if they had nothing to do but to make provision for the flesh to fulfil the lusts of it. Those who make a god of themselves, and a god of their bellies, in pride and wantonness, and cannot bear to be told of it, thereby forsake God, and show they esteem him lightly. There is but one way of a sinner's acceptance and sanctification, however different modes of irreligion, or false religion, may show that favourable regard for other ways, which is often miscalled candid. How mad are idolaters, who forsake the Rock of salvation, to run themselves upon the rock of perdition!
[Deut.32.19-Deut.32.25]
Verses 19-25
The revolt of Israel was described in the foregoing verses, and here follow the resolves of Divine justice as to them. We deceive ourselves, if we think that God will be mocked by a faithless people. Sin makes us hateful in the sight of the holy God. See what mischief sin does, and reckon those to be fools that mock at it.
[Deut.32.26-Deut.32.38]
Verses 26-38
The idolatry and rebellions of Israel deserved, and the justice of God seemed to demand, that they should be rooted out. But He spared Israel, and continues them still to be living witnesses of the truth of the Bible, and to silence unbelievers. They are preserved for wise and holy purposes and the prophecies give us some idea what those purposes are. The Lord will never disgrace the throne of his glory. It is great wisdom, and will help much to the return of sinners to God, seriously to consider their latter end, or the future state. It is here meant particularly of what God foretold by Moses, about this people in the latter days; but it may be applied generally. Oh that men would consider the happiness they will lose, and the misery they will certainly plunge into, if they go on in their trespasses! What will be in the end thereof? [Jer.5.31] Jer 5:31. For the Lord will in due time bring down the enemies of the church, in displeasure against their wickedness. When sinners deem themselves most secure, they suddenly fall into destruction. And God's time to appear for the deliverance of his people, is when things are at the worst with them. But those who trust to any rock but God, will find it fail them when they most need it. The rejection of the Messiah by the Jewish nation, is the continuance of their ancient idolatry, apostacy, and rebellion. They shall be brought to humble themselves before the Lord, to repent of their sins, and to trust in their long-rejected Mediator for salvation. Then he will deliver them, and make their prosperity great.
[Deut.32.39-Deut.32.43]
Verses 39-43
This conclusion of the song speaks, 1. Glory to God. No escape can be made from his power. 2. It speaks terror to his enemies. Terror indeed to those who hate him. The wrath of God is here revealed from heaven against them. 3. It speaks comfort to his own people. The song concludes with words of joy. Whatever judgments are brought upon sinners, it shall go well with the people of God.
[Deut.32.44-Deut.32.47]
Verses 44-47
Here is the solemn delivery of this song to Israel, with a charge to mind all the good words Moses had said unto them. It is not a trifle, but a matter of life and death: mind it, and you are made for ever; neglect it, and you are for ever undone. Oh that men were fully persuaded that religion is their life, even the life of their souls!
[Deut.32.48-Deut.32.52]
Verses 48-52
Now Moses had done his work, why should he desire to live a day longer? God reminds him of the sin of which he had been guilty, for which he was kept from entering Canaan. It is good for the best of men to die repenting the infirmities of which they are conscious. But those may die with comfort and ease, whenever God calls for them, notwithstanding the sins they remember against themselves, who have a believing prospect, and a well-grounded hope of eternal life beyond death.

Moses blesses the tribes and describes God's majesty (verses 1–5)

Moses added a solemn blessing to all his previous instructions, warnings and prophecies.

He began by recalling the Lord's glorious appearance when he gave the law.

God's law works like fire.

When accepted, it softens hard hearts, warms and purifies them, burning away corrupt desires.

When rejected, it hardens, burns and destroys.

The Holy Spirit descended upon the church in divided tongues like fire.

The gospel is also a fiery law.

When God's law is written on a person's heart, it is evidence that divine love has been poured into that heart.

We should regard God's law as one of the gifts of his grace.

Moses blesses the tribes (verses 6–23)

The tribes were not blessed in the usual order.

The blessing pronounced on Judah may refer to the tribe as a whole or to David, who foreshadowed Christ.

Moses gave a particularly full blessing to Levi.

In our religious service, the greatest goal should be acceptance with God, whether other people approve of us or not (2 Corinthians 5:9).

Henry understands this blessing as a prophecy that the Lord will continue supplying ministers to his church until the end of time.

Benjamin's inheritance was close to Mount Zion.

Living near the appointed means of worship was a precious gift that should not be exchanged for any worldly benefit or pleasure.

We should gratefully receive the earthly gifts God sends through the seasons.

But his spiritual gifts are immeasurably greater.

They come from the Father of lights, through Christ the Sun of Righteousness, and through the Holy Spirit's influence like the rain that makes the earth fruitful.

These are the signs of God's special love: the Spirit's gifts, grace and comfort.

When Moses prayed for the favor of the One who dwelt in the burning bush, he recalled the covenant, which is the foundation of every hope we have of God's favor.

God assigns people their places to live and wisely directs them toward different occupations for the common good.

Whatever our situation or work, it is both wise and right to apply ourselves to it and be content.

We should not merely invite other people into God's service.

We should also abound in it ourselves.

The blessing on Naphtali leads Henry to a final observation: God's favor alone can satisfy the soul.

Those who have it are truly happy, and they recognize that in possessing it they need nothing more.

Strength for each day (verses 24 and 25)

For true believers, all their circumstances can be made holy.

When they travel along a difficult road, God equips them with the readiness that comes from the gospel of peace.

“As your days, so shall your strength be.”

In Scripture, a day can mean the events and troubles that take place during it.

The promise is that God will continually and graciously sustain his people through whatever burdens or trials he appoints.

It belongs to all Abraham's spiritual descendants.

If they have work to do, they will be given strength for it.

If burdens are laid upon them, God will provide what they need to carry them.

He will never allow them to be tested beyond the strength he supplies.

The incomparable blessing of belonging to God (verses 26–29)

No people had a God like Israel's God.

The blessings proclaimed over Israel can also be applied to the spiritual church.

No people have a better dwelling place. Those who make God their home receive the comfort and protection of his presence (Psalm 91:1).

No people receive firmer support. God's everlasting arms hold up his people when they are brought very low.

His grace prevents their spirits from collapsing and their faith from failing (2 Corinthians 12:9).

No people are better governed. Through the Christ who loves them, believers become more than conquerors over their spiritual enemies.

No people enjoy better security. Israel can dwell safely, and those who remain close to God are protected by him.

No people receive a better inheritance. Every true Israelite looks by faith toward the heavenly Canaan, which contains better things than grain and wine.

No people have better help. In every danger or need, the eternal God is available to them.

Those whom he helps cannot finally be destroyed.

No people are better armed. Those who possess holiness in their hearts are defended by the complete armor of God (Ephesians 6).

No people have a surer promise of victory. The God of peace will soon crush Satan under believers' feet (Romans 16:20).

May the Lord help us set our hearts on things above, turning away from earthly possessions that will soon perish.

May we not share the hopelessness of Israel's enemies, but enter the realm of everlasting love and joy with God's true Israel.
classic_reading:
[Deut.33.1-Deut.33.5]
Chapter 33
Chapter Outline
The glorious majesty of God. | (1-5) |
The blessings of the twelve tribes. | (6-23) |
Strength to believers. | (24-25) |
The excellency of Israel. | (26-29) |
Verses 1-5
To all his precepts, warnings, and prophecies, Moses added a solemn blessing. He begins with a description of the glorious appearances of God, in giving the law. His law works like fire. If received, it is melting, warming, purifying, and burns up the dross of corruption; if rejected, it hardens, sears, pains, and destroys. The Holy Spirit came down in cloven tongues, as of fire; for the gospel also is a fiery law. The law of God written in the heart, is a certain proof of the love of God shed abroad there: we must reckon His law one of the gifts of his grace.
[Deut.33.6-Deut.33.23]
Verses 6-23
The order in which the tribes are here blessed, is not the same as is observed elsewhere. The blessing of Judah may refer to the whole tribe in general, or to David as a type of Christ. Moses largely blesses the tribe of Levi. Acceptance with God is what we should all aim at, and desire, in all our devotions, whether men accept us or not, [2Cor.5.9] 2Co 5:9. This prayer is a prophecy, that God will keep up a ministry in his church to the end of time. The tribe of Benjamin had their inheritance close to mount Zion. To be situated near the ordinances, is a precious gift from the Lord, a privilege not to be exchanged for any worldly advantage, or indulgence. We should thankfully receive the earthly blessings sent to us, through the successive seasons. But those good gifts which come down from the Father of lights, through the rising of the Sun of righteousness, and the pouring out of his Spirit like the rain which makes fruitful, are infinitely more precious, as the tokens of his special love. The precious things here prayed for, are figures of spiritual blessing in heavenly things by Christ, the gifts, graces, and comforts of the Spirit. When Moses prays for the good will of Him that dwelt in the bush, he refers to the covenant, on which all our hopes of God's favour must be founded. The providence of God appoints men's habitations, and wisely disposes men to different employments for the public good. Whatever our place and business are, it is our wisdom and duty to apply thereto; and it is happiness to be well pleased therewith. We should not only invite others to the service of God, but abound in it. The blessing of Naphtali. The favour of God is the only favour satisfying to the soul. Those are happy indeed, who have the favour of God; and those shall have it, who reckon that in having it they have enough, and desire no more.
[Deut.33.24-Deut.33.25]
Verses 24-25
All shall be sanctified to true believers; if their way be rough, their feet shall be shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace. As thy days, so shall thy strength be. The "day" is often in Scripture put for the events of the day; it is a promise that God would graciously and constantly support under trials and troubles, whatever they were. It is a promise sure to all the spiritual seed of Abraham. Have they work allotted? They shall have strength to do it. Have they burdens appointed? They shall have strength, and never be tempted above what they are able to bear.
[Deut.33.26-Deut.33.29]
Verses 26-29
None had such a God as Israel. There is no people like the Israel of God. What is here said of the church of Israel is to be applied to the spiritual church. Never were people so well seated and sheltered. Those who make God their habitation, shall have all the comforts and benefits of a habitation in him, [Ps.91.1] Psa 91:1. Never were people so well supported and borne up. How low soever the people of God are at any time brought, everlasting arms are underneath them, to keep the spirit from sinking, from fainting, and their faith from failing. Divine grace is sufficient for them, [2Cor.12.9] 2Co 12:9. Never were people so well commanded. Thus believers are more than conquerors over their spiritual enemies, through Christ that loved them. Never were people so well secured and protected. Israel shall dwell in safety alone. All who keep close to God, shall be kept safe by him. Never were people so well provided for. Every true Israelite looks with faith to the better country, the heavenly Canaan, which is filled with better things than corn and wine. Never were people so well helped. If in danger of any harm, or in want of any good, they had an eternal God to go to. Nothing could hurt those whom God helped, nor was it possible the people should perish who were saved by the Lord. Never were people so well armed. Those in whose hearts is the excellency of holiness, are defended by the whole armour of God, Ep 6. Never were people so well assured of victory over their enemies. Thus shall the God of peace tread Satan under the feet of all believers, and shall do it shortly, [Rom.16.20] Ro 16:20. May God help us to seek and to set our affections on the things above; and to turn our souls from earthly perishing objects; that we may not have our lot with Israel's foes in the regions of darkness and despair, but with the Israel of God, in the realms of love and eternal happiness.

Moses views Canaan from Mount Nebo (verses 1–4)

Moses had shown no desire to abandon his work before it was completed.

But once his work was finished, he showed no unwillingness to die.

God had made clear that Moses would not enter Canaan.

Yet the Lord also promised that he could see the land.

He gave him a view of the whole good country.

Believers sometimes receive a similar glimpse, through grace, of the happiness and glory prepared for them.

God may reserve the brightest discoveries of his kindness for his people near the end of life, to strengthen them as they die.

Those who die believing in Christ and hoping for heaven can leave this world joyfully.

Moses dies and Israel mourns (verses 5–8)

Moses obeyed God's command to die as willingly as the other commands he had received, though it might seem harder than any of them.

In this he resembled our Lord Jesus.

Yet there was a profound contrast.

Moses died peacefully, with honor, and without severe physical suffering.

Jesus died on a shameful and agonizing cross.

Moses died at the mouth of the Lord, according to God's command.

God's servants, when all their other work is done, must finally die.

They should be prepared to return home whenever their Master calls (Acts 21:13).

No one knew the place where Moses was buried.

If the soul is at rest with God, the place where the body lies matters comparatively little.

Moses' bodily strength had not failed.

His mind remained clear and active, and his memory was as strong as ever.

Henry regards this as a reward for his service and remarkable meekness.

Israel mourned solemnly for him.

But even after great losses, we must not allow grief to consume us.

If we hope to go joyfully to heaven, why should we approach the grave with nothing but sorrow?

Joshua succeeds Moses; Christ is greater than both (verses 9–12)

Moses brought Israel to the borders of Canaan and then died.

This pictured a deeper truth: the law makes nothing perfect (Hebrews 7:19).

It brings sinners into the wilderness of conviction but cannot bring them into the settled rest and peace of the heavenly Canaan.

That work belongs to Joshua, whose name is the same as the name of our Lord Jesus.

Joshua was a picture of him.

What the law could not accomplish, Jesus accomplished (Romans 8:3).

Through him we receive peace of conscience now and everlasting rest in heaven.

Moses was greater than every other Old Testament prophet.

Yet Jesus was greater than Moses by far more than Moses surpassed the prophets who came before or after him.

Notice the likeness between Israel's redeemer and the Redeemer of humanity.

Moses was sent by God to free Israel from cruel bondage.

He led the people out and overcame their enemies.

He became their deliverer, lawgiver and judge, bringing them to the very edge of the promised land.

Jesus came to rescue us from slavery to the devil and restore us to freedom and happiness.

He confirmed every moral command God had first given.

But he also writes the law, not upon stone tablets, but upon the living tablets of our hearts.

He will judge humanity.

God has appointed a day when Christ will expose the secrets of every person and reward or punish each one with perfect justice.

Because he is so much greater than Moses, we who follow Christ should obey him faithfully and live consistently with the holy faith we profess.

May God graciously enable us all to do so!
classic_reading:
[Deut.34.1-Deut.34.4]
Chapter 34
Chapter Outline
Moses views the promised land from mount Nebo. | (1-4) |
The death and burial of Moses, The mourning of the people. | (5-8) |
Joshua succeeds Moses, The praise of Moses. | (9-12) |
Verses 1-4
Moses seemed unwilling to leave his work; but that being finished, he manifested no unwillingness to die. God had declared that he should not enter Canaan. But the Lord also promised that Moses should have a view of it, and showed him all that good land. Such a sight believers now have, through grace, of the bliss and glory of their future state. Sometimes God reserves the brightest discoveries of his grace to his people to support their dying moments. Those may leave this world with cheerfulness, who die in the faith of Christ, and in the hope of heaven.
[Deut.34.5-Deut.34.8]
Verses 5-8
Moses obeyed this command of God as willingly as any other, though it seemed harder. In this he resembled our Lord Jesus Christ. But he died in honour, in peace, and in the most easy manner; the Saviour died upon the disgraceful and torturing cross. Moses died very easily; he died "at the mouth of the Lord," according to the will of God. The servants of the Lord, when they have done all their other work, must die at last, and be willing to go home, whenever their Master sends for them, [Acts.21.13] Ac 21:13. The place of his burial was not known. If the soul be at rest with God, it is of little consequence where the body rests. There was no decay in the strength of his body, nor in the vigour and activity of his mind; his understanding was as clear, and his memory as strong as ever. This was the reward of his services, the effect of his extraordinary meekness. There was solemn mourning for him. Yet how great soever our losses have been, we must not give ourselves up to sorrow. If we hope to go to heaven rejoicing, why should we go to the grave mourning?
[Deut.34.9-Deut.34.12]
Verses 9-12
Moses brought Israel to the borders of Canaan, and then died and left them. This signifies that the law made nothing perfect, [Heb.7.19] He 7:19 It brings men into a wilderness of conviction, but not into the Canaan of rest and settled peace. That honour was reserved for Joshua, our Lord Jesus, of whom Joshua was a type, (and the name is the same,) to do that for us which the law could not do, [Rom.8.3] Ro 8:3. Through him we enter into the spiritual rest of conscience, and eternal rest in heaven. Moses was greater than any other prophet of the Old Testament. But our Lord Jesus went beyond him, far more than the other prophets came short of him. And see a strong resemblance between the redeemer of the children of Israel and the Redeemer of mankind. Moses was sent by God, to deliver the Israelites form a cruel bondage; he led them out, and conquered their enemies. He became not only their deliverer, but their lawgiver; not only their lawgiver, but their judge; and, finally, leads them to the border of the land of promise. Our blessed Saviour came to rescue us out of the slavery of the devil, and to restore us to liberty and happiness. He came to confirm every moral precept of the first lawgiver; and to write them, not on tables of stone, but on fleshly tables of the heart. He came to be our Judge also, inasmuch as he hath appointed a day when he will judge all the secrets of men, and reward or punish accordingly. This greatness of Christ above Moses, is a reason why Christians should be obedient and faithful to the holy religion by which they profess to be Christ's followers. God, by his grace, make us all so!
